claims.text: Tribological performance of HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices initially improves as ambient temperature rises from room temperature to approximately 300°C.
The proposed improvement below approximately 300°C is caused by tribochemical oxides acting as solid lubricants.
Tribological performance degrades significantly above approximately 300°C.
Accelerated oxidation, matrix softening, and loss of coating adhesion cause the proposed high-temperature degradation.
The initial coating can be a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory HEA film on 304 stainless steel with high hardness.
Annealing improves the CuMoTaWV coating's adhesion and wear response.
The coating is exposed to test temperatures from room temperature through 600°C while sliding against a steel counterball.
The sliding tests are conducted in air at constant load and sliding velocity.
Temperature-dependent tribochemical layers can contain CuO, Fe2O3, and Cr2O3.
Increasing temperature changes dislocation mobility and diffusion rates in the HEA lattice.
Below 300°C, the HEA retains high hardness and develops a thin protective oxide that lowers friction and wear.
Above 300°C, accelerated oxidation produces thick, brittle oxide scales.
Above 300°C, accelerated diffusion thermally softens the HEA matrix.
High-temperature tribochemical reactions increase the coefficient of friction and wear rate.
The thermal transition is governed by competition between beneficial oxide lubrication and detrimental oxidation and softening.
Wear rate increases nonlinearly with temperature and exhibits a sharp increase above approximately 300°C.
The degradation boundary is approximately 300°C, with COF exceeding 1.0 and wear rate exceeding 2.5×10^-5 mm^3/N m beyond that boundary.
At room temperature, the annealed coating has a COF of approximately 0.25 and a wear rate of approximately 6.4×10^-6 mm^3/N m.
Wear changes from steady-state low abrasive wear at room and moderate temperatures to severe adhesive or oxidative wear at higher temperatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says performance initially improves as temperature rises toward 300°C, whereas the predicted outcome says wear rate increases nonlinearly with temperature without specifying an initial improvement regime.

The proposed beneficial regime extends to roughly 300°C and degradation is described as occurring beyond 300°C, but the stated values already worsen substantially at 300°C: COF rises from about 0.25 at room temperature to 1.5 and wear rate from 6.4×10^-6 to 2.5×10^-5 mm^3/N m.

The mechanism associates elevated temperature with thick brittle scales and severe wear, while the cited same-system observation at 300°C is described as low abrasive wear and film stability; the hypothesis does not clearly distinguish whether 300°C belongs to the protective or severe-wear regime.
